newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans in devastated Bunia say rebels take mines.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans in devastated Bunia say rebels take mines.

text.p: Picking through charred and looted buildings, residents of the eastern Zairean town of Bunia described on Thursday how rebels defeated government forces in fierce fighting and went on to capture nearby gold mines.
"The fighting was terrible and there were bodies all over the streets, those of us who had not already fled to the forest had to stay in our homes," said teacher Pierre Lolo.
"We are only glad it is quiet now and the army has gone. They can never come back here."
Bunia fell to rebels trying to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko after a 12 hour battle on December 24. Rebels say 307 government soldiers were killed while their own forces sustained 75 casualties.
Bunia is the greatest strategic advance made by Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces in several weeks, with its all-weather airport and significant nearby gold reserves.
Residents confirmed earlier rebel claims that the Kilo-Moto gold mining area 80 km (50 miles) from Bunia had fallen into their hands.
Last month Kabila ordered gold miners, including foreign holders of concessions, to come forward and discuss the future of their operations by January 3 or risk losing their assets.
With the capture of Bunia the predominantly ethnic Tutsi rebels hold a swath of eastern Zaire over 600 km (400 miles) long bordering Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
The rebels hope to use income from Zairean minerals and commodities like coffee to fund their rebellion.
The fighting in Bunia was heaviest around the airport and the town centre bears more the ravages of systematic looting over a period of three weeks than those of battle.
Small groups of people drift quietly along the dusty main street, picking up what they can salvage or just looking and glad to be still alive.
Everything of value which could be carried away has gone.
Windows are smashed and doors hang loose on their hinges. Some shops were torched before the army left and the soot-blackened shells stand out like rotten teeth.

"The soldiers began looting on December 2, and that was when many people ran away, then they started to accuse us of being rebels and if they caught more than five people together they were immediately accused," said businessman Emmanuel Mambala.
"If you couldn't pay them then you would be killed, and many people were."
Bunia was once a relatively wealthy town in an impoverished region. People have begun returning from the forests where they hid during the fighting, and where the army is rumoured to have fled.

At least two days drive from the main border town of Goma, down a forest road through pygmy villages with potholes as deep as a car, confirmation of the fall of Bunia took a long time to filter through.
